Salesforce is a cloud-based CRM platform that provides comprehensive tools for managing customer data, business logic, and automated workflows [1][2][3].

API authentication is handled primarily via OAuth 2.0 with PKCE [1][4][5]. API access is generally not gated; developers can sign up for a free Salesforce Developer Edition to access and test APIs [4]. The API surface includes REST API, GraphQL API, Tooling API, and various specialized Connect APIs [2]. Salesforce officially supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) through its Hosted MCP Servers feature, which enables AI agents to interact with Salesforce data and logic [1][6].

The main blocker to building an integration is typically the granularity of the API surface; if internal APIs or custom tools require a specific sequence of multiple calls to be useful, they may perform poorly with AI agents that lack the context to chain them correctly [6].

Official resources:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/apis [2]
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/hosted-mcp-servers/guide/hosted-mcp-servers-overview.html [1]

HubSpot is a customer platform that provides software, services, and support to help businesses grow [1].

API authentication methods include OAuth 2.0 (required for multi-account distribution), static access tokens for private single-account installations, and developer API keys for specific features [2]. Service keys (in beta) are also available for direct REST API access [3].

API access is not gated by self-serve; you can create a free developer account to gain immediate access to test portals and public APIs [1]. The API surface includes REST APIs [4], webhooks [4], and a HubSpot CLI for local development [2][4]. Official SDKs are provided for Node.js [2][5].

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is officially supported via two distinct servers: a remote server for AI agents to interact with CRM data [6][7] and a local server for agentic development tools to interact with the Developer Platform [6].

The main challenge when building integrations is the requirement for a hosted OAuth backend service when distributing apps to multiple accounts [2].

Official resources: https://developers.hubspot.com/docs/apps/developer-platform/build-apps/authentication/overview [2], https://developers.hubspot.com/docs/api-reference/latest/overview [8], and https://developers.hubspot.com/ai-tools/mcp [6].

Slack is a collaboration platform providing messaging, file sharing, and workflow automation. It uses OAuth 2.0 (including confidential OAuth for MCP) and bearer tokens for API authentication [1][2][3]. API access is not self-serve gated in the sense of a manual approval barrier for internal apps, though public distribution requires mandatory review and approval via the Slack Marketplace [4]. Slack supports REST-like Web APIs, Events API, Socket Mode, SDKs (Node.js, etc.), and CLI [5][2][3][6]. MCP is officially supported via the Slack MCP server [1][4]. A primary integration blocker is mandatory Marketplace review for public apps [4]. 

Official documentation: https://api.slack.com, https://docs.slack.dev [4].

GitHub is a developer platform for version control, collaboration, and workflow automation [1]. 

API authentication is handled via personal access tokens (classic or fine-grained), GitHub App tokens, or the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN in Actions [2][3]. Basic authentication using a client ID and secret is supported for some app-specific endpoints [2]. API access is not self-serve gated; it is available to users and apps [2][1][4]. The API surface includes REST [1], GraphQL [4], official Octokit SDKs [1], CLI [3], and webhooks [1]. Model Context Protocol (MCP) is officially supported via the GitHub MCP Server [5][6]. Integration blockers typically involve missing required permissions or scope scopes [2][6].

Documentation: [https://docs.github.com/en/rest](https://docs.github.com/en/rest), [https://docs.github.com/en/graphql](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql), [https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server](https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server) [1][5][4].

Stripe is a financial infrastructure platform that provides a unified set of APIs for accepting payments, managing billing, and building financial workflows [1]. Authentication is handled via API keys using HTTP Basic Auth or Bearer Token headers [2][3]. API access is self-serve; you can manage keys and interact with sandboxes directly through the dashboard [2][4][3]. The API surface is primarily REST-based, supported by official server-side SDKs, a CLI, and webhooks [1][4][5]. Model Context Protocol (MCP) is officially supported via a dedicated server [6]. Integration complexity primarily involves managing API key security and versioning [2][7][3].
